# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 24 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 24 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_024_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 4, Chapter 3

**1** I asked her about the four colors on the beast's head. She replied, "You are eager about these things again." "Yes, my lady — tell me what they mean." **2** "The black represents this present world in which you live. **3** The fiery and blood-red means that this world must be destroyed by blood and fire. **4** The golden part represents you and all those who flee from this world. For just as gold is refined by fire and becomes useful, so you who dwell in this world are being refined. Those who remain and pass through the flames will be purified by them. Just as gold sheds its dross, so you will shed all sorrow and anguish, and you will be purified and fit for the building of the tower. **5** The white part represents the coming age, in which the chosen of God will dwell. For those chosen by God will be spotless and pure, and the life of the age to come will be radiant. **6** Therefore do not cease speaking these things into the ears of the saints. You have been given the foreshadowing of the great tribulation to come — but if you are willing, it will amount to nothing. Remember everything that has been written before." **7** When she had said these things she departed, and I could not see in which direction she went; there was a noise, and I turned around in fear, thinking the beast was coming.

---

### Council Notes

The four-color eschatological scheme:
- **Black** = this present age (dark, passing)
- **Fiery/blood-red** = the destruction that ends this age (fire and blood)
- **Golden yellow** = the elect in the process of being refined through tribulation
- **White** = the age to come (pure, radiant, spotless)

The gold-refinement metaphor (v. 4) is the Shepherd's most developed statement on suffering: tribulation is not punitive but purifying. The believer emerges from it refined and useful — like gold without dross.

Hermas's involuntary fear at a noise (v. 7) is a memorable ending — the encounter with the beast has left its trace on his body even after it has been overcome in faith. The Shepherd never spiritualizes away the physical reality of fear.
